facts.fact: A share of stock is a small piece of ownership in a company, so a stockholder owns part of the business and shares in its gains or losses.
facts.hook: a grandparent gives a teen one share of a sneaker company, and the teen wonders whether that means free shoes

facts.fact: A bond is a loan from an investor to a government or company, which promises to pay interest and to repay the original amount on a set date.
facts.hook: at a bank, a kid is confused that the savings bond they were given counts as a loan they made

facts.fact: If a company goes bankrupt, its bondholders must be paid back before its stockholders, who are last in line and often receive nothing.
facts.hook: two cousins argue over whether the stock or the bond of a failed toy company is worth keeping

facts.fact: A company can cut or skip the dividends it pays stockholders, but missing a promised interest payment on its bonds counts as a default.
facts.hook: a teen's stock stops paying its small dividend, while her brother's bond from the same company keeps paying

facts.fact: If a company fails completely, its stock price can fall to zero, so a stockholder can lose every dollar they put in.
facts.hook: a friend who bet all his birthday money on one hyped company learns what 'zero' looks like

facts.fact: Over the past century, U.S. stocks have earned higher average yearly returns than U.S. government bonds, but with much bigger drops along the way; the extra return rewards the extra risk.
facts.hook: a class investing game splits into a stock team and a bond team, and the lead keeps changing hands

facts.fact: When interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds fall, because buyers can get new bonds that pay more interest.
facts.hook: a teen tries to sell an old low-interest bond and finds nobody will pay full price for it

facts.fact: U.S. Treasury bonds are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government and are considered among the safest investments in the world.
facts.hook: a grandparent explains why she keeps her emergency savings in Treasury bonds instead of stocks

facts.fact: Bonds from borrowers more likely to fail to pay are called high-yield or 'junk' bonds, and they must pay higher interest to attract lenders.
facts.hook: a student spots a bond paying twice the usual interest and has to figure out what the catch is

facts.fact: Buying a fund that holds many different stocks, called diversifying, means one company's collapse hurts much less than if all the money were in that one stock.
facts.hook: two friends compare what happened when one company crashed: one owned only that stock, the other owned a fund

facts.fact: After the 1929 crash, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell about 89 percent from its September 1929 peak to its low in July 1932.
facts.hook: a history project on a great-grandparent's lost savings makes stock risk suddenly feel real

facts.fact: A bond held until its maturity date pays back its full face value, as long as the issuer does not default, no matter how its price moved in between.
facts.hook: a teen panics when her bond's price dips, until she checks when it matures

facts.fact: The law of demand says that when the price of something rises, people buy less of it, as long as nothing else changes.
facts.hook: at a farmers' market, a stand doubles its strawberry price and the line suddenly disappears

facts.fact: The law of supply says that when the price of something rises, sellers offer more of it, because producing it becomes more profitable.
facts.hook: after strawberry prices jump, a kid notices three new berry stands at the market the next week

facts.fact: The equilibrium price is the price at which the amount buyers want to buy equals the amount sellers want to sell.
facts.hook: two kids running a fruit stand keep adjusting their sign until they sell out right at closing time

facts.fact: Where strawberries ripen outdoors in early summer, a flood of local berries raises the supply all at once, which usually pushes their price down.
facts.hook: a kid is amazed that summer strawberries at the market cost half what they did in March

facts.fact: In winter, strawberries sold in cold regions are usually trucked or flown in from warmer places, and the cost of that transport helps make them pricier.
facts.hook: a grocery trip for a winter birthday cake turns into a question about why berries cost so much

facts.fact: Florida produces about three-quarters of the United States' winter strawberries, harvesting mainly from December through March.
facts.hook: a kid reads the label on a January strawberry carton and wonders how they grew in winter

facts.fact: If a price is held below the equilibrium price, buyers want more than sellers will offer, and the result is a shortage.
facts.hook: a class sale prices strawberry cups too low and runs out in five minutes, leaving a long angry line

facts.fact: If a price is held above the equilibrium price, sellers offer more than buyers want, and unsold goods pile up as a surplus.
facts.hook: a lemonade stand's pricey strawberry lemonade leaves them with jugs of it at the end of the day

facts.fact: Fresh strawberries spoil within days of picking, so a grower with too many cannot store them for later and often has to cut the price to sell them.
facts.hook: at closing time a farmer slashes her strawberry price, and a kid figures out why

facts.fact: When one good gets expensive, some buyers switch to a substitute, such as blueberries in place of strawberries, which lowers demand for the pricier good.
facts.hook: a family planning a fruit salad swaps in cheaper fruit when strawberries are too expensive

facts.fact: A frost, hailstorm or drought that ruins part of a strawberry crop reduces the supply, which pushes the price of the remaining berries up.
facts.hook: after a late frost, a kid's favorite berry stand posts a much higher price

facts.fact: British economist Alfred Marshall popularized the supply-and-demand diagram, with its two crossing curves, in his 1890 book Principles of Economics.
facts.hook: a student drawing the crossing curves for homework wonders who first made them famous

facts.fact: Simple interest is paid only on the original amount deposited, called the principal, so it adds the same dollar amount every year.
facts.hook: a kid checks a savings statement and notices the interest is exactly the same every year

facts.fact: Compound interest is paid on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so the interest itself starts earning interest.
facts.hook: at the bank, a teen learns her interest payment grew a little even though she added nothing

facts.fact: At 5 percent simple interest, $1,000 earns $50 a year, so after five years the account holds $1,250.
facts.hook: a grandparent offers to hold a teen's $1,000 for five years at 5 percent simple interest

facts.fact: At 5 percent interest compounded once a year, $1,000 grows to $1,276.28 after five years.
facts.hook: a teen compares the grandparent's offer with a bank paying 5 percent compounded yearly

facts.fact: The simple interest formula is I = P x r x t: interest equals the principal times the yearly rate times the number of years.
facts.hook: a student checks a bank's advertised interest with a pencil and the formula

facts.fact: With interest compounded once a year, the balance after n years equals P x (1 + r) to the power n, where r is the yearly rate as a decimal.
facts.hook: a kid uses a calculator's power key to see what their savings will be at graduation

facts.fact: At the same yearly rate, interest compounded monthly grows a little faster than interest compounded yearly, because each month's interest starts earning sooner.
facts.hook: two bank ads offer the same rate, and a teen has to spot why one pays slightly more

facts.fact: The rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double with compound interest: divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate, so about 12 years at 6 percent.
facts.hook: a teen wonders how old they will be when their savings doubles

facts.fact: In the United States, the Truth in Savings Act of 1991 requires banks to state savings rates as an annual percentage yield, or APY, which includes the effect of compounding.
facts.hook: a kid notices a bank poster lists both an interest rate and a slightly higher APY

facts.fact: On a graph, a simple-interest balance rises in a straight line, while a compound-interest balance curves upward, gaining more each year than the year before.
facts.hook: a math class plots two savings accounts and sees the lines slowly pull apart

facts.fact: The saying that compound interest is 'the eighth wonder of the world' is often credited to Albert Einstein, but there is no reliable evidence he ever said it.
facts.hook: a student about to quote Einstein in a presentation checks the source first

facts.fact: If prices rise faster than a savings account's interest rate, the money in the account buys less each year even though the balance grows.
facts.hook: a teen's savings grew for five years, yet it no longer covers the bike it once would have

facts.fact: A contour line on a topographic map joins points that are all at the same height above sea level.
facts.hook: at home, a kid planning a hike with a grandparent traces one wiggly brown line all the way around a hill

facts.fact: Where contour lines are packed close together the ground is steep; where they are spread far apart the slope is gentle.
facts.hook: two friends choose a trail up a hill and one insists the route with crowded lines will be brutal

facts.fact: The contour interval is the difference in height between one contour line and the next, and it is printed in the map's legend.
facts.hook: a kid miscalculates a hill's height until they read the tiny note in the map's legend

facts.fact: On many topographic maps, usually every fifth contour line is drawn thicker and labeled with its elevation; these are called index contours.
facts.hook: a hiker counting lines one by one learns a faster way from the thick labeled ones

facts.fact: Contour lines for different heights never cross each other, because one spot cannot have two elevations; at a vertical cliff they may touch or merge.
facts.hook: a student drawing a map for a project realizes two of their lines crossed and something is wrong

facts.fact: A set of closed loops, one inside another, shows a hill, and the smallest loop in the middle marks the top.
facts.hook: friends race to find the summit on a map before they start climbing

facts.fact: Where contour lines cross a stream, they bend into a V shape that points uphill, toward the stream's source.
facts.hook: a kid figuring out which way a creek flows notices the Vs in the contour lines

facts.fact: A closed contour loop with short tick marks pointing inward, called hachures, shows a hollow or depression rather than a hilltop.
facts.hook: a hiker expecting a lookout point on the map finds a sunken pond instead

facts.fact: Slope steepness can be found by dividing the rise in height by the horizontal distance; rising 100 meters over 500 meters is a 20 percent grade.
facts.hook: a cyclist uses a map to work out whether a road hill will be too steep to ride

facts.fact: Contour lines spaced evenly apart show a slope that has the same steepness all the way along it.
facts.hook: a sledding crew hunts on a map for a slope that won't suddenly get steeper

facts.fact: The U.S. Geological Survey's standard 7.5-minute topographic maps use a scale of 1:24,000, so one inch on the map equals 2,000 feet on the ground.
facts.hook: a kid measuring a trail on a grandparent's old map with a ruler needs to convert inches to distance

facts.fact: On U.S. Geological Survey topographic maps, contour lines are printed in brown.
facts.hook: a kid unfolding a map at home wonders what all the thin brown squiggles mean

facts.fact: The word monsoon comes from the Arabic word mawsim, meaning 'season', because a monsoon is a wind that reverses direction with the seasons.
facts.hook: at a travel agency, a family wonders why the brochure warns about 'monsoon season'

facts.fact: In summer, land heats up faster than the ocean, so warm air rises over the land and moist air from the ocean flows in to replace it.
facts.hook: a kid visiting relatives in India asks why the rain arrives right when the heat is worst

facts.fact: In winter, South Asia's winds reverse and blow mostly from the land out to sea, bringing the region's dry season.
facts.hook: a family booking a trip to India learns why winter there is sunny and dry

facts.fact: India's summer monsoon is called the southwest monsoon because its moist winds blow in mostly from the southwest, across the Arabian Sea.
facts.hook: at an airport, a kid watches a weather map arrow and asks why it points from the sea

facts.fact: The India Meteorological Department gives June 1 as the normal date for the southwest monsoon to reach Kerala, on India's southwestern coast.
facts.hook: a grandparent in Kerala marks early June on the calendar every year and explains why

facts.fact: The southwest monsoon season, June through September, brings roughly three-quarters of India's yearly rainfall.
facts.hook: a kid on a video call hears that a whole year's rain mostly falls in four months

facts.fact: Mawsynram, in India's Meghalaya state, is often called the wettest place on Earth, averaging nearly 12 meters of rain a year.
facts.hook: at a travel agency, a teen spots a trip to the 'wettest place on Earth' and has questions

facts.fact: Rice is usually grown in flooded fields called paddies, and the standing water helps keep many weeds from growing.
facts.hook: a kid sees photos of rice fields that look like shallow lakes and wonders why

facts.fact: In South Asia, crops sown at the start of the summer monsoon and harvested in autumn are called kharif crops, and rice is the main one.
facts.hook: a grandparent who farmed in Punjab explains why planting waited for the first big rains

facts.fact: Rice seedlings are often grown first in a small nursery bed and then transplanted, often by hand, into flooded paddy fields.
facts.hook: a kid visiting a farm is surprised that rice gets planted twice

facts.fact: When the monsoon arrives late or brings too little rain, rice planting is delayed and harvests can shrink, which can push food prices up.
facts.hook: a family notices rice costing more at their grocery after news of a weak monsoon

facts.fact: In northern summer, the rainy band of rising air near the equator, called the Intertropical Convergence Zone, shifts north over South Asia and helps bring monsoon rains.
facts.hook: a student comparing satellite images from January and July sees the cloud band move north

facts.fact: Latitude measures how far north or south a place is from the equator, from 0 degrees at the equator to 90 degrees at each pole.
facts.hook: at a travel agency, a kid tries to guess which city on a list is closest to the equator

facts.fact: Longitude measures how far east or west a place is from the prime meridian, from 0 degrees up to 180 degrees east or west.
facts.hook: a kid at an airport reads coordinates on a flight screen and can't tell which number is which

facts.fact: The prime meridian, at 0 degrees longitude, was set through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London, by an international conference held in Washington, D.C., in 1884.
facts.hook: a kid on a London trip stands on a line at Greenwich and asks why the world's zero is there

facts.fact: By convention, a location's latitude is written first and its longitude second, as in about 40 degrees north, 74 degrees west for New York City.
facts.hook: two friends swap the numbers in a map app and end up looking at the wrong place

facts.fact: Each degree of latitude or longitude is divided into 60 minutes, and each minute into 60 seconds, to pinpoint an exact spot.
facts.hook: a kid sees 'minutes' on a map coordinate and assumes it has to do with time

facts.fact: One degree of latitude covers about 111 kilometers, or about 69 miles, of north-south distance.
facts.hook: a kid estimates how far a grandparent's hometown is by counting degrees on a map

facts.fact: Lines of longitude meet at the poles, so a degree of longitude spans about 111 kilometers at the equator but shrinks to zero at the poles.
facts.hook: a student on a globe notices the longitude lines squeezing together near the top

facts.fact: Lines of latitude are also called parallels because they never meet, and lines of longitude are called meridians.
facts.hook: a kid reading an old atlas at a grandparent's house hits the words 'parallel' and 'meridian'

facts.fact: Quito, the capital of Ecuador, lies less than a quarter of a degree south of the equator, so its latitude is almost zero.
facts.hook: at a travel agency, a teen finds a capital city with a latitude that starts with zero

facts.fact: In the decimal coordinates used by GPS and online maps, latitudes south of the equator and longitudes west of the prime meridian are written as negative numbers.
facts.hook: a kid drops a minus sign typing coordinates and the map lands on the other side of the world

facts.fact: Earth turns 15 degrees of longitude every hour, which is why time zones are roughly 15 degrees wide.
facts.hook: at an airport, a kid works out the time back home from how far east they flew

facts.fact: In 1714 the British Parliament offered a prize of up to 20,000 pounds for a practical way to find a ship's longitude at sea.
facts.hook: a student wonders why sailors could find latitude easily but needed a prize to solve longitude

facts.fact: A climate graph usually shows each month's average temperature as a line and each month's average rainfall as bars on the same chart.
facts.hook: at home, a kid tries to read a climate graph and first mistakes the bars for temperature

facts.fact: A desert is often defined as a place that gets less than about 250 millimeters, or 10 inches, of rain a year.
facts.hook: a kid is surprised to learn a cold, snowy place can count as a desert by its rainfall

facts.fact: In the Koppen climate system, a tropical rainforest climate has every month averaging at least 18 degrees Celsius and at least 60 millimeters of rain.
facts.hook: a student checks each month on a climate graph to decide if a city counts as rainforest

facts.fact: A rainforest climate graph shows a nearly flat temperature line, because temperatures there stay warm and change little from month to month.
facts.hook: at a travel agency, a teen asks which month is best for a rainforest trip and finds they all look alike

facts.fact: In tropical rainforests, the difference between day and night temperatures can be larger than the difference between the warmest and coolest months.
facts.hook: a kid packing for a rainforest trip is told to bring a sweater for nights despite the steady yearly heat

facts.fact: Parts of Chile's Atacama Desert are so dry that some weather stations there have never recorded rain.
facts.hook: a student makes a desert climate graph where some bars are simply missing

facts.fact: Many of the world's hot deserts lie near 30 degrees north or south of the equator, where sinking air warms up and dries out.
facts.hook: a kid on a globe notices the big deserts line up in two belts

facts.fact: Tropical rainforests lie near the equator, where strong sunlight heats moist air that rises, cools and forms clouds, often bringing heavy afternoon rain.
facts.hook: a traveler's photos from the Amazon show blue skies each morning and storms each afternoon

facts.fact: Two climate graphs can only be compared by bar height if their rainfall axes use the same scale; otherwise a short bar may stand for more rain.
facts.hook: two classmates argue over which city is wetter until one checks the axis numbers

facts.fact: Desert rainfall is not just low but unreliable: a desert may go years with almost no rain and then get a heavy downpour in a single storm.
facts.hook: a kid wonders why a desert town has flood warning signs

facts.fact: In hot deserts, the sun and dry air could evaporate far more water in a year than falls as rain, so the ground stays dry.
facts.hook: a kid's puddle experiment in a desert backyard vanishes before lunch

facts.fact: The Koppen climate classification, still used on climate maps today, was developed by Wladimir Koppen, a climatologist born in Russia who worked in Germany.
facts.hook: a student sees letter codes like 'Af' and 'BWh' on a climate map and looks up who invented them

facts.fact: Anxiety is a normal feeling of worry or fear, but it may be an anxiety disorder when it is intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life.
facts.hook: a kid wonders whether a friend's constant worrying before tests is normal nerves or something more

facts.fact: Anxiety can show up in the body as a racing heart, fast breathing, stomachaches, headaches or trouble sleeping.
facts.hook: a friend keeps visiting the school nurse with stomachaches on the same day every week

facts.fact: A person with anxiety may start avoiding places or activities that worry them, such as school, parties or sports practice.
facts.hook: a teammate who never missed practice starts making excuses every time

facts.fact: Other signs of anxiety can include irritability, trouble concentrating, restlessness and asking again and again for reassurance.
facts.hook: a best friend texts the same worried question five times, and a kid starts to notice a pattern

facts.fact: Anxiety triggers the body's fight-or-flight response, releasing adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and breathing even when there is no real danger.
facts.hook: a friend's heart pounds before reading aloud in class, and they ask why their body acts like it's in danger

facts.fact: A panic attack is a sudden surge of intense fear that peaks within minutes and can feel like a heart attack, even though it is not one.
facts.hook: at a doctor's office, a teen learns what really happened when a friend thought they couldn't breathe

facts.fact: A large U.S. survey of teens aged 13 to 18 found that about a third had had an anxiety disorder at some point, the most common kind of mental disorder among them.
facts.hook: a kid who feels alone with a friend's worries learns how common anxiety really is

facts.fact: Trusted adults a young person can tell about a worried friend include a parent, teacher, school counselor, school nurse or doctor.
facts.hook: a kid at a grandparent's house finally decides who to talk to about a friend who seems scared all the time

facts.fact: If a friend talks about hurting themselves, it is important to tell a trusted adult right away, even if the friend asked you to keep it a secret.
facts.hook: a kid torn between a promise of secrecy and a friend's safety chooses to tell a counselor

facts.fact: In the United States, calling or texting 988 reaches the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, which began on July 16, 2022.
facts.hook: a kid notices a poster about 988 at a doctor's office and remembers it later

facts.fact: Anxiety disorders are treatable, and cognitive behavioral therapy, which teaches people to notice and change anxious thoughts, is one of the most effective treatments.
facts.hook: a friend who got help from a counselor explains what their sessions are like

facts.fact: Telling an anxious friend to 'just calm down' rarely helps; listening without judging and taking their worry seriously usually helps more.
facts.hook: a kid's first attempt to help a panicking friend backfires, so they try just listening

facts.fact: When smoke is inhaled, nicotine reaches the brain within about 10 seconds.
facts.hook: at a doctor's office, a teen asks why her uncle reaches for a cigarette the moment he gets stressed

facts.fact: Nicotine works by fitting into nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, proteins on brain cells that normally respond to the brain's own chemical messenger, acetylcholine.
facts.hook: a science-fair partner compares nicotine to a fake key that fits the brain's lock

facts.fact: Nicotine causes brain cells in the reward pathway to release dopamine, a chemical messenger linked to pleasure and motivation.
facts.hook: a kid asks a grandparent who quit smoking why it was so hard to stop

facts.fact: The brain's main reward pathway runs from the ventral tegmental area, deep in the brain, to the nucleus accumbens, and addictive drugs boost dopamine along it.
facts.hook: a student labels a brain diagram for a health project on addiction

facts.fact: Dopamine release teaches the brain that a behavior is worth repeating, which is how nicotine use becomes a learned habit.
facts.hook: a teen compares the pull of nicotine to how they keep checking their phone for likes

facts.fact: Nicotine's effects fade quickly because the body clears about half of it in roughly two hours, so users soon feel the urge for another dose.
facts.hook: a kid notices an older cousin who vapes getting restless every couple of hours

facts.fact: With regular use, the brain adapts to nicotine, so a person needs more of it to feel the same effect; this is called tolerance.
facts.hook: at a pharmacy, a pharmacist explains to a teen why a relative's habit keeps growing

facts.fact: When a dependent person stops using nicotine, withdrawal can bring irritability, anxiety, trouble concentrating and strong cravings.
facts.hook: a kid's parent is grumpy all week after quitting, and the family learns why

facts.fact: Places, people and routines linked with nicotine use, such as a certain time of day, can become cues that trigger cravings on their own.
facts.hook: a grandparent who quit years ago admits morning coffee still makes them think of cigarettes

facts.fact: According to the CDC, nearly 9 out of 10 adults who smoke cigarettes daily first tried smoking by age 18.
facts.hook: a health class discusses why tobacco companies' interest in teenagers matters

facts.fact: The brain keeps developing until about age 25, which makes young people more vulnerable to nicotine addiction than adults.
facts.hook: a teen tells a friend offering a vape that their brain is still under construction

facts.fact: Nicotine is named after Jean Nicot, a French ambassador to Portugal who sent tobacco to Paris in 1560.
facts.hook: a student researching the word 'nicotine' finds a person's name hidden in it

facts.fact: Puberty usually begins between ages 8 and 13 in girls and between 9 and 14 in boys, and starting anywhere in that range is normal.
facts.hook: a kid worried about being the last in class to change asks the doctor what is normal

facts.fact: Puberty is driven by hormones: the pituitary gland in the brain signals the ovaries or testes to make more estrogen or testosterone.
facts.hook: at a doctor's office, a kid asks what actually tells the body it's time for puberty

facts.fact: During puberty, sweat glands in the armpits and groin called apocrine glands become active and start producing sweat.
facts.hook: a kid notices their gym shirt smells in a way it never did last year

facts.fact: Fresh sweat has almost no smell; body odor comes from bacteria on the skin breaking down sweat.
facts.hook: two friends argue whether sweat itself stinks after a hot soccer game

facts.fact: Antiperspirants reduce sweating by using aluminum compounds that temporarily plug the sweat ducts.
facts.hook: at a pharmacy, a kid is confused by two nearly identical sticks with different labels

facts.fact: Deodorants do not stop sweat; they fight odor by slowing the growth of skin bacteria and covering smells with fragrance.
facts.hook: a kid who uses deodorant is puzzled that their shirt still gets damp

facts.fact: Hormones during puberty make the skin's oil glands produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and cause acne.
facts.hook: a kid finds their first pimple before school photos and wants to know where it came from

facts.fact: According to the American Academy of Dermatology, about 85 percent of people between ages 12 and 24 get at least minor acne.
facts.hook: a kid embarrassed about acne learns at the doctor's office how many people their age have it too

facts.fact: Showering with soap, especially after exercise, washes away the sweat and bacteria that cause body odor.
facts.hook: a kid who skipped a shower after practice notices classmates edging away

facts.fact: Sweat and bacteria stay in worn clothes and socks, so changing into clean ones each day helps prevent body odor.
facts.hook: a kid realizes their smelly hoodie, not their armpits, is the problem

facts.fact: During puberty the larynx, or voice box, grows larger and the vocal cords get longer and thicker, which makes the voice deeper, especially in boys.
facts.hook: a boy's voice cracks in the middle of a class presentation and he wonders why

facts.fact: Squeezing or popping pimples can push bacteria deeper into the skin and can leave scars.
facts.hook: a kid about to pop a pimple before a party gets a warning from an older sibling
